newsitem.title: USA: Most U.S. Treasuries end narrowly higher.
newsitem.headline: Most U.S. Treasuries end narrowly higher.

text.p: Most U.S. Treasury prices ended narrowly higher on Wednesday, participants said.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond closed at 94-14/32, up 1/32, to yield 7.07 percent.

Prices lost ground early on, hurt by a Washington Post interview with Federal Reserve Vice Chairman Laurence Meyer in which Meyer said that the "the economy is really strong" and that this was "not a fluke." Then "an extremely hawkish story" on Bridge News sent prices to session lows, analysts said.
Bridge News interviewed "senior Fed sources" who said the U.S. economy would need more interest rate increases if growth is to moderate enough to keep inflationary pressures in check.
A strengthening dollar lent the Treasury market support, analysts said.

"The dollar did better ... and that spilled over and pushed us off the lows we reached after the Bridge News story that moved the market the lower," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.
The market had a fairly light calendar of economic news to contend with. The government reported that factory orders rose 0.8 percent in February, somewhat less than economists had forecast.
But General Motors said car and truck sales rose in March.
"The figures we got suggested spending in the auto markets is holding its own," said Flanagan.

The Treasury announced that it would sell $8.0 billion in inflation-indexed notes on April 8. That news had very little influence on the market, said Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities Inc.

Volatile stock market trading attracted some attention, traders said. With the Dow at times down more than 100 points, "we were watching the equity market," said Kevin Sluder, senior government trader at First Chicago Capital Markets. "People kept an eye on equities more than anything else."
Foreign central banks were said to have bought five-year notes and a hedge-fund bought two-years, traders said.
But besides eyeing stock market gyrations, participants were looking ahead to the March employment report, due Friday.
"We're waiting for Friday," said Sluder. Dimick agreed.
"I don't think we're going to move very far from here until the payroll numbers print," he said.

Sluder said a lot of different components of the March employment report could affect the market on Friday. If jobs grow moderately and wage increases are fairly contained, then the 30-year bond yield could fall to seven percent and the two-year yield could fall to 6-1/4 percent, he said. But if the data show robust job and wage gains, bond yields could rise to 7.20 percent or 7.25 percent and two-year note yields could reach 6.50 percent or 6.55 percent.
"The big item is the wage component," said Flanagan.

"Given the market's oversold condition, I wouldn't be surprised to see some buying if the employment report isn't overly robust," he said. "But if you got a nickel gain or better in hourly wages, it would be tough for the market to get overly enthusiastic."
At the short end of the maturity curve, three-month bill rates eased one basis point to 5.15 percent. Six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.30 percent.
Year bill rates slipped two basis points to 5.63 percent while two-year note prices were unchanged at 99-23/32, yielding 6.40 percent.
The five-year note climbed 1/32 to 99-20/32 to yield 6.71 percent and the ten-year was up 2/32 at 95-20/32 to yield 6.87 percent.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
